processing: Little is documented; as is typical of Chinese green tea, the leaf is fixed by heat, shaped and dried.
harvest_season: Early spring; the county's climate brings the buds on early. Exact dates are little documented.
appearance_dry: Well-made strips with a glossy, bright green colour and a substantial feel in the hand.
appearance_liquor: As with other early-picked Chinese greens, a clear pale yellow-green.
appearance_wet: As is typical of spring green tea, soft tender leaf in fresh green.
taste_profile: Little is documented about its flavour; expect what is typical of early-spring Chinese green tea, fresh, lightly vegetal and softly sweet.

brewing.notes: General guidance for a tender spring green: use a glass or porcelain vessel and water well off the boil, and do not leave the buds stewing.

vintage_note: Sold like other spring greens, by the current year's harvest, and best drunk within about a year. Check the picking season on the pack rather than the region name alone.
description:
Sanjiang tea comes from Sanjiang Dong Autonomous County in northern Guangxi, near where Guangxi, Hunan and Guizhou meet. It is a protected regional name, and its selling point is earliness: the county's warm, humid climate in the Nanling range brings the buds on early.

Little is published about its method here, so assume the usual green tea steps of heat fixing, shaping and drying. Light handling suits young leaf, keeping the shape and colour intact.

There is not much detailed tasting writing about it, so treat this as a guide from its class: fresh, gently vegetal and softly sweet is what a good early-spring Chinese green should deliver. Cooler water and modest steeps protect it. Boiling water is the usual way to make a tender green turn bitter.

At the shop, ask for the picking season and the year. This is a large producing area, and the regional name covers a wide range of quality, so the picking grade tells you more than the label. A cold brew is worth trying too, since local tastings have promoted it that way.
history:
The firm part of the record is modern: Sanjiang tea became a nationally protected geographical indication product in 2012.

In 2024 it was one of 44 geographical indications named to a national protection project list. Reported figures for 2023 give about 215,000 mu of tea gardens and 23,000 tonnes of dry tea.
